name: voiceless dental fricative

articulation.tongue_position: Tongue tip placed between upper and lower front teeth, or against the back of the upper teeth
articulation.airflow: Continuous airflow forced between tongue and teeth, creating friction
articulation.voicing: Voiceless — vocal cords do not vibrate

common_errors.explanation: Speakers produce a dental/alveolar stop instead of a fricative — tongue blocks air rather than allowing continuous flow
Speakers use the closest fricative in their L1 — the tongue stays behind the teeth instead of between them
Labiodental fricative substituted — lower lip touches upper teeth instead of tongue between teeth

practice_sentences: I think the three brothers went through the thick forest.
Both math problems have something in common.

name: voiced dental fricative

articulation.tongue_position: Same as /θ/ — tongue tip between or against upper teeth
articulation.airflow: Continuous airflow with friction, same as /θ/
articulation.voicing: Voiced — vocal cords vibrate (place hand on throat to feel)

common_errors.explanation: Voiced stop replaces voiced fricative — tongue completely blocks air instead of allowing friction
Voiced alveolar fricative — correct voicing but wrong tongue position

practice_sentences: The mother and father gathered together in the weather.
This and that are over there with the others.

name: alveolar approximant (English R)

articulation.tongue_position: Tongue tip curled back (retroflex) or bunched in the middle of the mouth, NOT touching the roof
articulation.airflow: Air flows smoothly around the tongue without friction

common_errors.explanation: L1 has a single liquid phoneme between English /r/ and /l/ — the key distinction is whether tongue TOUCHES (l) or DOESN'T TOUCH (r) the alveolar ridge
Lip rounding without tongue curling
Uvular fricative from L1 — produced too far back in the throat

practice_sentences: The red car drove right around the corner.
Three great trees grew near the river.

name: alveolar lateral approximant

articulation.tongue_position: Tongue tip touches the alveolar ridge (bump behind upper front teeth). Air flows around the SIDES of the tongue.
articulation.airflow: Lateral — air escapes around the sides of the tongue

common_errors.explanation: L1 liquid sound is between /r/ and /l/ — for English /l/, the tongue tip MUST touch the ridge
Both are alveolar — the difference is /n/ sends air through the nose, /l/ sends air around tongue sides

practice_sentences: Let me tell you a little story about the long lake.
Please pull the light blue lever on the left.

name: voiced labiodental fricative

articulation.tongue_position: Tongue is not involved — this is a LIP sound
articulation.airflow: Upper teeth lightly touch the inner part of the lower lip, air is forced through creating friction
articulation.lip_position: Lower lip pulled slightly inward to touch upper teeth

common_errors.explanation: Hindi /v/ is a labiodental approximant (no teeth contact) — English /v/ requires teeth-on-lip friction
Bilabial stop — both lips come together instead of teeth touching lip
Same lip position but voiceless — only difference is vocal cord vibration

practice_sentences: I have a very vivid view of the valley.
Every evening, seven doves visit the village.

name: velar nasal

articulation.tongue_position: Back of tongue presses against the soft palate (velum) — same position as /k/ or /g/
articulation.airflow: Air flows through the NOSE (not the mouth) — the mouth is blocked

common_errors.explanation: Alveolar nasal instead of velar — tongue touches the front ridge instead of the back of the mouth
Adding a hard /g/ after the nasal — 'sing' becomes 'sing-g'. The /ŋ/ should end without a stop.

practice_sentences: I was singing a song in the morning.
Something interesting is happening this evening.

name: near-open front unrounded vowel

articulation.tongue_position: Tongue low and pushed forward in the mouth
articulation.airflow: Open vowel — no constriction, air flows freely
articulation.lip_position: Spread (corners pulled back slightly), mouth open wider than for /ɛ/

common_errors.explanation: Not opening the mouth wide enough — /æ/ requires more jaw opening than /ɛ/ (as in 'bed')
Too far back — /æ/ is a FRONT vowel, tongue should be forward

practice_sentences: The happy cat sat on the man's hat.
The family traveled to a fantastic land.

name: voiceless postalveolar fricative

articulation.tongue_position: Tongue blade raised toward the area just behind the alveolar ridge (postalveolar)
articulation.airflow: Continuous friction — air is channeled into a groove along the center of the tongue

common_errors.explanation: Alveolar fricative — tongue too far forward and lips not rounded enough
Adding a stop before the fricative — should be continuous friction, not a burst

practice_sentences: She went to the shop to buy a fresh fish.
The English machine was shipped to the nation.

name: voiced postalveolar affricate

articulation.tongue_position: Tongue starts pressed against the postalveolar ridge (like /d/), then releases into /ʒ/ friction
articulation.airflow: Starts as a stop (blocked), then releases into a fricative (friction) — a combination sound

common_errors.explanation: Fricative only, missing the initial stop — French 'j' is just /ʒ/, English 'j' starts with tongue pressed up
Palatal approximant — too soft, missing the stop and friction components

practice_sentences: The judge made a large gesture from the edge of the stage.
Just imagine a magic journey to a gentle jungle.

name: Consonant Clusters in English
common_spelling: str, spl, nts, sts, ths, etc.

articulation.tongue_position: Varies — each consonant in the cluster must be articulated individually without inserting vowels between them
articulation.airflow: Transitions smoothly between consonants without pausing or adding sounds
articulation.voicing: Varies per consonant in the cluster

common_errors.explanation: Many languages don't allow complex consonant clusters. Speakers insert a short vowel (epenthesis): 'street' → 'sitareet', 'speak' → 'espeak'
Dropping one consonant from the cluster: 'strengths' → 'strengs', 'texts' → 'texs'

practice_sentences: The strong stream splashed against the spring rocks.
She read three texts about the strengths of the structure.
